title: API and Security Primer
description: Learn trust boundaries, validation, identity, permission, and safe data handling before authentication phases.

lessons.title: Trust Boundaries and Untrusted Input
lessons.summary: Any value crossing from browser/client/external service should be considered untrusted until validated/verified.
lessons.body:
Trust Boundaries and Untrusted Input

Why this matters
Any value crossing from browser/client/external service should be considered untrusted until validated/verified. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Any value crossing from browser/client/external service should be considered untrusted until validated/verified.
• Frontend validation improves UX but cannot enforce server security because callers can bypass the UI.
• A boundary should parse/validate shape before business code assumes types/required fields.
• Database constraints and authorization are separate checks, not replacements for validation.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, api and security primer stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter trust boundaries and untrusted input again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

Introduce one safe failure and diagnose the cause systematically.

Write the expected behavior in one sentence before adding code.

example.code:
Scenario: User B sends a request for User A's task.

Untrusted:
- URL task id
- request body
- role claimed by the browser

Trusted only after server verification:
- authenticated subject
- database-backed membership/ownership

Expected result: 403 and unchanged data.

lessons.title: Authentication vs Authorization
lessons.summary: Authentication establishes identity evidence; authorization evaluates whether that identity may perform an action on a resource.
lessons.body:
Authentication vs Authorization

Why this matters
Authentication establishes identity evidence; authorization evaluates whether that identity may perform an action on a resource. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Authentication establishes identity evidence; authorization evaluates whether that identity may perform an action on a resource.
• A valid token does not imply permission to every record.
• Resource ownership/membership checks prevent IDOR even when route IDs are guessable.

lessons.title: Secrets, Public Configuration, and Environment Boundaries
lessons.summary: A secret is valuable because unauthorized possession grants capability; treat keys/passwords/tokens accordingly.
lessons.body:
Secrets, Public Configuration, and Environment Boundaries

Why this matters
A secret is valuable because unauthorized possession grants capability; treat keys/passwords/tokens accordingly. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• A secret is valuable because unauthorized possession grants capability; treat keys/passwords/tokens accordingly.
• Anything shipped to browser JavaScript must be considered public to the user.
• Environment variables are a delivery mechanism, not automatically secret if included in client bundles/logs.

lessons.summary: XSS executes attacker-controlled script in another user's browser context.

Common Web Risks in Plain Language

Why this matters

lessons.title: Security Testing Mindset
lessons.summary: Test what an attacker would change: IDs, roles, methods, fields, file names, content types, request rate, expired tokens.
lessons.body:
Security Testing Mindset

Why this matters
Test what an attacker would change: IDs, roles, methods, fields, file names, content types, request rate, expired tokens. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Test what an attacker would change: IDs, roles, methods, fields, file names, content types, request rate, expired tokens.
• Negative tests are first-class: the system must prove it rejects unauthorized/invalid operations.
• Logs should help diagnose abuse without recording passwords/tokens/private content unnecessarily.
• Security is layered risk reduction, not one library or final checklist.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, api and security primer stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter security testing mindset again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

Purpose
